doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Making A Great Day in Harlem
title: Music clearance and the Bourne and Ellington catalogue problems
summary: The Polka Dots and Moonbeams rights demand, most favored nations, and the Ellington catalogue owner who blocked a documentary.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: It’s a brute. But the worst in the music clearance. And there are 23 musical numbers in this movie. And there’s something called a “most favored nations.” And that means whichever publisher gets the most money gets matched by all the others. So we were going along trying to cut corners. Now we had to clear for overseas cable, regular television, theaters, festivals, all kinds of stuff. And so we shaved a few years off and did this and did that to make everything kind of come together, until the last tune. And that was Lester Young playing “Polka Dots and Moonbeams.” And it was gorgeous. And this horrible woman at Bourne Publishers, she’s the granddaughter of the founder, asked for a hundred thousand dollars. Well I got furious. And I figured she wanted to play with me, you know, that she’d come down two thousand and I’d go up one thousand from five thousand, which I’d planned to pay her. I mean it was just awful. And so we took it out of the film. But I felt we put something else in which worked even better, with “Stardust” and it was kind of the repeat of something earlier in the film. But I was talking to Gerry Mulligan’s first wife, Arlene, whose father was Lou Brown of DeSilva, Brown and Henderson. And she said, “boy if they did anything like that about my father’s songs, I’d be furious,” because she wants them played you know. I said I’ll bet the widow VanHeusen doesn’t know that they’re doing this to her late husband’s music. And so someday, justice will prevail. Oh, listen, I’ve got a friend who made the best documentary I’ve ever seen on Ellington, and you’ll never see it unless you caught it that one time it was on PBS. Because the man who has all the Ellington music that Ruth got rid of, I mean Ellington left her the catalogue— © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

Yes, she sold to a man named Fox. And he’s like this person at Bourne. He wants the moon. And this poor guy, I was going to get him before I got Matthew, to see if he’d want to work on the film. And I never could — I saw him once and he said, “yeah it sounded wonderful.” But I never could get him on the phone. He always had a cold or he was having a nervous breakdown. Because he’s got this treasure and he can’t—
That’s too bad because it stifles things to come out of it that might come later.

Yeah. And this was such a good piece on Ellington. But you couldn’t, there’s no way you could do it without music, although I think he should figure something out, because it’s so full of information. It’s just great.
